en: Seeking to obey Kobosh,
Openly firing upon you,
He had lost the one he relied upon,
Yrchy-uul and Bozuul—
We lost those two.
In madness, we forty companions
Attacked you.
Bereft of our comrades,
May we forty companions perish—
We have become rabid!
May the night of Qadr be
We have fallen into your hands, my orphan;
There is no daylight for us apart from you.
If you wish, leave us alive;
If you grow wrathful,
Here are the forty companions—slaughter us!
We have no garden established in Talas,
No time to lie sprawled at ease.
No garden established in Keng-Kol,
The forty companions taken captive
Have no time to lie at leisure!”
The forty companions cried aloud,
“Of Manas, gone to Judgment,
The spirit!” they sobbed.
When he saw the forty companions,
Semetey, son of the mighty one,
Bent his knees to the earth;
From Taibuurul’s back
He sprang down in haste.
“From my father gone to the other world,
The support I have inherited,
My dear forty uncles!
For whose sake did I return?
For the strong-backed Kyrgyz people,
And my journey was for your sake!
My shelter, which the lion relied upon,
From my father gone to the other world,
The good fortune I inherited.
When I send you ahead, my auspicious path;
The support left by my father—
When I lead you, my countless army.
If they see my child,
Against the seething unbelievers,
When you charge, you satisfy my longing.
Having all twelve khans
Twelve times against Beijing,
When I fight, you satisfy my longing.
My cliff too high for geese to circle,
The support left by my father
He has now placed in my hands.
I can give myself to You, my God!
From my royal father, the fierce hero,
My heart's support, left by Manas,
My cause is more righteous than all;
The forty companions are my mirror!
If the forty companions are beside me,
Into darkening Beijing
I shall go straight and level my spear.
The grim-faced Chinese—
I shall slaughter them all, leaving none!
Against Kakan Chin’s Beijing
I shall wage a mighty campaign.
I shall wreak havoc upon Beijing.
If you are my support, forty companions,
I shall avenge the blood of my khan father Manas!
When horses grow fat and strong,
When men grow fat and restless,
Beijing, land of Kakan-Chyn—
That is the people I must fight.
Against the darkly looming Manchus,
If we march straight in and wreak slaughter,
From that hell of grievous hardship,
If we free our poor souls!
Against Beijing, untouched by the Four Companions,
If I do not clash in battle,
That place where my forefather died,
If I do not pursue his blood-price to the end!
Breaking their ranks with spears,
If death comes by God's will,
Struck by a bullet in mighty Beijing.
To Beijing, where Chalyar would not go,
If we do not charge and wage war,
Against the Kara-Khitai and Manchus
If I do not avenge this boundless grudge,
Against Beijing of Chyn-Machyn,
Against the people of true China,
Against those infidels swarming like black spiders,
How many heroes have vengeance to take
Against the warrior Khan Kongurbai!
He is our grievance when we come to dispute,
He is our enemy when we come to fight.
There are the people of Kakan-Chyn;
Against that people whom we must face,
I, the orphan, have a grievance.
Khan Bakai and Khan Sary—
If I do not have them take up the banner,
Against the Manchus and Chinese from the flank,
If I do not bring slaughter upon them,
My falcon father Manas—
If I do not thus avenge him!
My dear forty uncles!
Along the road you yourselves have known,
Along the valleys' springs and streams,
There are the Kalmak and Shibee peoples,
And that fine fellow, Khan Kongurbai.
The Kyrgyz and Kalmaks joined together,
With their custom of fighting.
My dear forty uncles,
Listen carefully:
My words carry this much weight.
Consider it, forty uncles:
Does not a mortal person die?
The Creator's command—
Does not His poor servant meet it?
Breaking their ranks with spears,
Struck by a bullet when death comes,
Dying when our appointed end arrives,
Let us meet them in battle;
Against the Chinese of Kapsang-Too,
Let us fight and bring upheaval.
If you will stand by me, forty uncles,
Against the seething Chinese,
Let us unleash turmoil!
There are the mines of Altyn-Too;
If we clash with the Kara-Khitai,
They have a strong support behind them:
Their great lion on whom they rely,
Their champion, Bek Kongurbai.
If we advance and make war,
We have seven forefathers to avenge.
In Beijing, beyond the reach of the Flood,
There are ravines no one has seen,
There are mountains where tea is gathered.
All their famous men, every one,
My father cut down;
Only Kongurbai remains his foe.
In the war of former days,
In those events,
When my father took the Kakan,
Among the seething Chinese,
When he unleashed turmoil,
When my khan father became sultan
And ruled for six months,
Many sorrows remain in the heart;
Such is this treacherous world.
Taking wives in that place,
Of the Muslim people
A people called Targana remained.
'We will campaign against the Kakan!'
And Kyrgyz descent
A people remained who said, 'Let us attack!'
Forty companions left by my father,
Let us reckon the days,
Let us put the month in writing.
Regaining flesh and strength, let us act,
Gathering our handful of Muslims,
Mustering them into a force.
Gathering all the Muslim people,
Against grim-faced Beijing,
If we do not fight to the last,
Upon the Chinese, numerous as a cow's hairs,
If we do not bring great hardship,
On the seething Kara-Khitai,
If we do not charge and avenge ourselves,
Let us die rather than live!
There is an enemy we must engage;
Let us try facing them.
I have drawn upon tradition,
I have asked the knowledgeable.
There are your white-bearded elders,
My uncle Bakai and all the rest,
There are giants among the Muslim people,
Many lions, all together.
Once, the infidels and Muslims
Came into conflict over this,
Standing opposite one another,
Thrusting and grappling with spears,
Fighting at the cost of their lives.
My father, Khan Manas,
Beijing, untouched by the Four Companions—
When he fiercely attacked it,
When he went against the famed Kakan's Beijing,
When he went there to fight,
Struck from the flank,
All the mighty men
Taking a gift to China.
The khan who went with news died;
Against Beijing of Kakan-Chyn,
Everyone who challenged it died.
Elebei and Khan Jeeren died,
The hero Bokmurun died too,
Muzburchak and Khan Kokcho died;
Of the Chinese of Chyn-Machyn,
Everyone they encountered died.
Going to the Kakan and returning,
My leopard father died too,
Bereft of those dear men;
Ak-Kula was shot down,
Almambet became a martyr,
The lions Syrgak and Serek died,
Baichoro, Bozuul, Agayar—
Their champions died alike.
Akbaltai's hero Chubak,
Amid the true slaughter,
Fought for six whole months,
Against the grim Kara-Khitai,
Until they were spent.
Until the pliant dry stalks ripened,
Until the autumn gossamer flew,
Until more than six months had passed,
He fought tirelessly for six months,
Lashing out like a lion.
Lion Chubak, the dauntless hero,
In the desert of It-Olbos,
The Chinese drums
He had applied to the wound.
When the battle raged in turmoil,
Was shot by Kojojash.
The sky was covered with cloud;
Struck by a bullet, Khan Chubak
Escaped like a coward,
Laying the whip on Kogala,
What could dauntless Chubak do?
He fled without stopping, galloping on,
His wound grew inflamed,
His flesh wasted away, leaving bone,
His blood drained away, leaving flesh,
His fine mustache lay smooth,
He was stricken with a terrible affliction,
His half-open eyes wandered wildly.
Sometimes he could speak,
Sometimes he could not speak,
Distressed, his eyes darted about.
Unable to find the road to Talas,
Unable to judge his way across the land,
That accomplished, dear hero Chubak,
I heard, lost his way.
Roaming the whole world,
He visited the shrines upon the earth,
Not leaving a single one out.
His consciousness was dim and dazed,
Sometimes lucid, sometimes mad,
That was how he lived.
What could dear Chubak do?
Like a fool, mad in the head,
Turning away then,
Finding no land like this Talas—
Look at God's decree!—
Finding no people like these Kyrgyz,
Roaming the whole world,
Wandering through Andijan.
Some people say
He went to Arslanbap;
Some people say
Synchybek of Andijan
Gave him a burning poison,
